| [LIT-035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-035.md) v2 | The ergodicity solution of the cooperation puzzle | Peters & Adamou (2022), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2020.0425. If N entities' resources follow GBM (drift μ, volatility σ, independent noise), then pooling and sharing equally every step leaves the drift at μ, cuts the volatility to σ/√N (Eq. 3.9), and raises each member's time-average growth rate from μ − σ²/2 to μ − σ²/(2N) (Eq. 4.1). The premium is (σ²/2)(1 − 1/N) (Eq. 4.2). With pairwise correlation ρ the effective volatility is σ√((1 + (N−1)ρ)/N), and the large-N limit is μ − σ²ρ/2 (Eqs. 5.12–5.13). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-059](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-059.md)); worth reading as the clearest short derivation of the risk-pooling (geometric-mean) advantage of sharing under multiplicative noise. The mathematics is correct and self-contained. The framing claim, that this "solves" the cooperation puzzle and makes cooperation the default, rests on the model's zero-cost, no-cheating assumptions, and the paper's own citations (McCloskey, Winterhalder, Uitdehaag, Kennedy et al.) show the core result was already known. |

Sole-authored survey by a condensed-matter physicist. It takes novelty (a property the parts lack) as the defining mark of emergence and sets it against twelve other characteristics in §2. The six "objective" ones are discontinuities, order, modification of parts, universality, diversity and mesoscale modularity. The six "subjective" ones are self-organisation, unpredictability, irreducibility, contextuality/downward causation, complexity and intra-stratum closure. Case studies from the Ising model to Schelling segregation and LLMs show that each can come apart from novelty: novelty without discontinuity (Kondo, Fermi liquids, spin ice), without unpredictability (BKT, spin ice), and with reduction (Butterfield). §22 sides with weak emergence and argues that strong-emergence claims from molecular structure are weak. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-124); worth reading as a hub reference and example catalogue on emergence from physics outward, with unusually concrete case studies and a sceptical physicist's §15 on molecular structure. | [LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md) | Plain Talk About Neurodevelopmental Epistemology | Minsky (1977), MIT AI Memo 430, also IJCAI-77 pp. 1083–1092. Read it for the communication scheme, the "specificity gradient", the case-shift mechanism and the conjecture that cognitive cases precede and shape linguistic ones; do not read it as evidence for any of them. | [LIT-402](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-402.md) | K-Lines: A Theory of Memory | Minsky (1979/1980), MIT AI Memo 516; Cognitive Science 4(2):117–133. "The function of a memory is to re-create a state of mind." On a memorable event a K-node is made, and its K-line attaches to the agents then active. Reactivated, it re-imposes that partial mental state, but by the level-band principle only on an intermediate band of levels, so the present is seen as an instance of the past without hallucinating the old answer. K-lines attach mainly to earlier K-nodes, forming a K-pyramid against the perceptual P-pyramid, and cross-exclusion lets conflicting details cancel into abstraction. Read from the memo; a programme statement, with no simulation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 from the MIT AI Memo 516 text ([NOTE-352](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-352.md)), not the Cognitive Science version, which was not reachable; worth reading as the society-of-mind programme's theory of memory and the first place Minsky's own text uses the phrase "Society of Mind". The idea to take away is that a memory re-creates a partial mental state rather than retrieving a stored description, and its level-band principle: re-enact only an intermediate band of the original state, so the present problem is seen as an instance of the remembered one. The second half is, by its author's account, not constructive ("from this point, the reader can assume that difficulties in understanding are my fault"), and nothing is simulated or measured. |

The Internet Archive scan is lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher or author copy of the book is posted. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md) | The Society of Mind | Minsky (1986), Simon & Schuster. The book-length statement of the Society of Mind programme, begun with Seymour Papert in the early 1970s. A mind is a society of many small agents, each mindless by itself, and intelligence comes from their diversity and organisation, not from one principle. The publisher presents it as a puzzle of self-contained one-page pieces that assemble into a theory. Unread: no lawful full text was reachable, so it is registered from the publisher's description and the contents list. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from the publisher's description, the Library of Congress catalogue record and the Google Books contents list, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive copies are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only, and Minsky's web page did not post the book. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. Its programme is read here at second hand through Singh's exposition ([LIT-444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-444.md)) and at first hand through the draft of its sequel ([LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md)). |
| [LIT-435](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-435.md) | The emergence of understanding in a computer model of concepts and analogy-making | Mitchell & Hofstadter (1990), DOI-10.1016/0167-2789(90)90086-5. The Physica D statement of Copycat, the Fluid Analogies Research Group's model of analogy-making in a microworld of letter strings, in which understanding is meant to emerge from many small, parallel, nondeterministic agents (codelets) interacting with a network of concepts (the Slipnet) under a computational temperature. Unread: what is said here comes from its co-authored companion paper [LIT-414](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-414.md), which cites it for the details of Copycat's "xyz" run. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from Crossref, the Elsevier metadata API and the account of Copycat in Chalmers, French & Hofstadter ([LIT-414](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-414.md), read in full), not read: the article is closed access at Elsevier, ScienceDirect returned 403, and no author or repository copy was found. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-436.md) | Intelligence without representation | Brooks (1991), Artificial Intelligence 47:139–159, written in 1987. Argues that AI should be built incrementally from complete autonomous "Creatures" tested in the real world, and that the system should be decomposed by activity into parallel layers, each connecting sensing to action, not by function into perception, a central reasoner and action. His robots have no central representation and no central control: each layer is a fixed network of simple finite-state machines, and a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing or inhibiting its wires. Coherent behaviour emerges, "in the eye of an observer", from competing behaviours. Hypothesis: representation is the wrong unit of abstraction for the bulk of intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md)) from the copy Brooks posts; worth reading as the decomposition side built and run: a robot whose purposive behaviour comes from parallel layers of simple finite-state machines with no central representation and no central control, which Brooks likens to Minsky's account of human behaviour. The coherence of the whole, he says, exists "in the eye of an observer". The evidence is three layers on one physical robot, described rather than measured. It makes no claim about minds or experience and disclaims interest in the philosophy. |
| [LIT-439](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-439.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition | Levin (2019), Frontiers in Psychology 10:2688. Proposes "Scale-Free Cognition": an Individual or Self is the set of parts that pursue a goal together, bounded by the farthest events in space and time it can measure and try to change (its "cognitive light cone"). Selves scale up from homeostatic loops through memory and anticipation, and cells merge into larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions; cancer is the boundary shrinking back to one cell. Because every level that pursues its own goal is a Self, most living systems hold many nested, coexisting Selves, "not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory". Levin's "Self" is a goal-pursuing collective, an agent and an individual in this record's terms; the essay gives no account of a self as subject. A hypothesis essay: no model and no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md)); worth reading as the composition-side statement that agency is nested by default: a Self is whatever set of parts pursues a goal together, so cells, organs, organisms and swarms are Selves at once, each bounded by its "cognitive light cone". It is a hypothesis-and-theory essay with no model, no measurement procedure for the light cone and no data of its own. Its one sentence against IIT's single-Self picture is asserted in a bracket, not argued, and its consciousness claims are confined to a closing speculation. |
| [LIT-444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-444.md) | Examining the Society of Mind | Singh (2003), Computing and Informatics 22(6):521–543. A sympathetic exposition of Minsky's Society of Mind by his student. It traces the theory's history: Minsky and Papert's 1970s copy-demo robot, the procedure-bearing frames of 1974, the abandoned 1976 book drafts, and the 1977 and 1980 papers. It catalogues the mechanisms and how agents communicate without shared symbols. It finds resemblances in Bayes nets, case-based reasoning, blackboards, Cyc, Soar and multiagent systems, none of which it calls a Society of Mind. Its verdict is that the theory has never been implemented. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-339.md)); worth reading as the shortest reliable map of The Society of Mind ([LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md)), written by the student who worked with Minsky on its sequel. It gives the theory's history from the 1970s memos, a catalogue of its mechanisms (agents and agencies, K-lines, nemes and nomes, frames and transframes, difference-engines, censors, A- and B-brains, ways agents communicate and grow), and a survey of later AI it resembles. It is an exposition, not a test: it reports no implementation and quotes the theory more than it argues for it. Its history leans on unpublished 1976 drafts that only the author saw. |
| [LIT-457](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-457.md) | Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies: A Review | Burns (1995), DOI-10.1609/aimag.v16i3.1155. A review of Hofstadter and FARG's Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies ([LIT-428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-428.md)). It finds two ideas under the book: cognition modelled by a parallel terraced scan of probabilistic codelets, and cognition as high-level perception. It asks why the work has had little impact on AI, and answers: microdomains, and critiques of rival programs that rest on analogy and intuition, applied to others but not to Copycat. It recommends the book. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-375](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-375.md)); worth reading as the one contemporary account the record holds of what is in [LIT-428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-428.md), which is unread, and as a short, fair statement of the two standing complaints against the Fluid Analogies programme: every model lives in a microdomain, and rival programs are dismissed by analogy and intuition while the same tests are waved off for Copycat. It is a three-page book review. Its account of the parallel terraced scan is clear and checkable; its verdict is the reviewer's opinion, argued with one worked example (symbol grounding in SME versus Copycat). |
| [LIT-498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-498.md) | The Evolution of Cooperation | Axelrod & Hamilton (1981), DOI-10.1126/science.7466396. In an iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with probability w of meeting again, TIT FOR TAT won two computer tournaments (14 and 62 entries) and an ecological simulation, and no strategy can do better against it when w ≥ max((T−R)/(T−P), (T−R)/(R−S)). ALL D is always stable; reciprocity can still enter through kinship or a cluster, after which a nice stable strategy resists clusters. Applications range from cleaner fish to disease and nondisjunction. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md)); worth reading as the formal statement of how reciprocity can start, spread and hold: tit-for-tat is robust in Axelrod's tournaments, cannot be bettered by any mutant when the continuation probability w is high enough, and can enter an all-defect population through kinship or clustering. "Evolutionarily stable" is stronger than what is proved: the proof shows no strategy does better than TIT FOR TAT, and always-cooperate does as well, which Boyd & Lorberbaum (1987) later turned into a proof that no pure strategy is evolutionarily stable in the repeated game. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation; it is not about morality. |
| [LIT-501](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-501.md) | Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation | Nowak (2006), DOI-10.1126/science.1133755. Five mechanisms let natural selection favour cooperators who pay c to give b: kin selection (r > c/b), direct reciprocity (w > c/b), indirect reciprocity (q > c/b), network reciprocity (b/c > k) and group selection (b/c > 1 + n/m). Each is cast as a 2×2 game, from which conditions for cooperators to be evolutionarily stable, risk-dominant or advantageous follow. Punishment is said not to be a mechanism. Cooperation is proposed as a third principle of evolution. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-409](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-409.md)), main text only; the online supplement with the derivations was not read. Worth reading as the standard short map of mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation (kin selection, direct, indirect and network reciprocity, group selection), each reduced to a benefit-to-cost threshold from a 2×2 game. Every mechanism is modelled with the donation game, so it covers altruism only: mutualism, coordination and conflict resolution, four of morality-as-cooperation's seven domains, are outside it. Its one sentence on morality credits indirect reciprocity with "the evolution of morality", citing Alexander (1987). |
| [LIT-506](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-506.md) | The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour. II | Hamilton (1964), J. Theor. Biol. 7:17–52. Part I's model is generalized, "unrigorously", into two principles: an animal values a neighbour's fitness against its own by their relationship, and its social discriminations evolve to make relationship more determinate. They are applied to alarm calls, clones and colonies, the haplodiploid hypothesis for hymenopteran sociality, multiple mating, fights between relatives, sibling competition and seed provisioning. Evidence is anecdotal, and the author reports where it runs against him. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-410](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-410.md)); worth reading as the place inclusive fitness is turned into two general principles (valuing neighbours by relatedness; evolving discrimination that makes relatedness determinate) and tried on warning behaviour, social insects, clones, fights and parental care. The principles are offered as an "unrigorous" generalization of Part I, and the evidence is anecdotal and, by the author's account, partly contrary. Its §6 on fights is the one place in Hamilton's pair that touches contests: relatives should fight less, a kin-weighted version of the restraint Maynard Smith and Price derived without kinship. |
| [LIT-515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-515.md) | Statistical physics of self-replication | England (2012; J. Chem. Phys. 2013), arXiv:1209.1179. For a system in a heat bath obeying detailed balance, a transition between coarse-grained ensembles I → II obeys β⟨ΔQ⟩ + ln π(II→I) + ΔS_int ≥ 0 (Eq. 6), a second law stated for macrostates. Applied to self-replication, the reverse probability is small when the copy is durable and made fast, so the heat released per copy is bounded below by about 2n ln(n τ_decay/τ_div) − ΔS_int (Eq. 8). The author's estimates put E. coli within a factor of three of this bound and a self-replicating RNA near it. The "self" in self-replication is an observer's classification of microstates, not a physical given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-419](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-419.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published J. Chem. Phys. text was not reached. Worth reading as the founding paper of the "dissipation-driven" programme and as a clean worked use of a macrostate fluctuation relation: the heat a replicator must release is bounded below by how fast it copies and how durable the copy is, not by the copying itself. The general bound (Eq. 6) is a coarse-grained second law and is sound; the numbers for E. coli and RNA rest on an argued, not derived, upper bound on the reverse probability (Eq. 7). It draws no line between living and non-living replicators, and says so: "self" is a classification an observer supplies. |
| [LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md) | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine (1977), Nobel Lecture, reprinted in Science 201:777 (1978). Near equilibrium the second-order excess entropy δ²S is a Lyapounov function, so fluctuations die out, and in the "strictly" linear regime the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium the sign of the excess entropy production ΣδJδX is no longer fixed. Given autocatalytic steps (necessary, not sufficient) the thermodynamic branch can go unstable, and fluctuations are amplified into "dissipative structures": Bénard convection, the Brusselator's limit cycle and "Turing bifurcation". A closing programme derives irreversibility from a non-unitary transformation of the Liouville dynamics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md)); worth reading as Prigogine's own short statement of the dissipative-structure programme, and as the place where its scope limits are stated in his words. A dissipative structure is a state beyond an instability of the "thermodynamic branch", "a giant fluctuation stabilized by exchanges of energy with the outside world". The minimum-entropy-production theorem is valid only in the "strictly" linear regime with constant phenomenological coefficients. Far from equilibrium the only general criterion offered is a sufficient one for stability (non-negative excess entropy production). Its §§6–7 programme of a non-unitary "entropy operator" is a sketch whose demonstrated link to macroscopic thermodynamics is, by its own account, "at least in the linear region". |
| [LIT-518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-518.md) | Statistical Physics of Adaptation | Perunov, Marsland & England (2014; Phys. Rev. X 2016), arXiv:1412.1875. Starting from a fluctuation relation between coarse-grained macrostates, the paper writes the log-odds of two outcomes of a driven system as an internal-entropy term, a reversal-probability term and Ψ − Φ, the mean heat minus a fluctuation correction (Eq. 8). Holding the first two fixed, the more likely outcome is the one whose formation absorbed and dissipated work from the drive more reliably. It calls such outcomes "adapted" and argues the tendency needs no self-replication. Two single-particle hopping models illustrate the dissipation and fluctuation terms (Eqs. 10–13); the many-body case is a plausibility argument. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-416](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-416.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published Physical Review X text was not reached. Worth reading as the origin of "dissipative adaptation": the claim that driven matter tends towards states whose formation absorbed and dissipated work reliably, with no replication needed. Read it as a heuristic argument with two toy models, not a theorem. Its exact content is a rearranged macrostate fluctuation relation; the step to "adaptation" holds two terms fixed that it does not show can be held fixed in a many-body system, and the simulation it reports was not shown. It deliberately erases the line between living and non-living organization. |
| [LIT-519](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-519.md) | Nonequilibrium thermodynamics and maximum entropy production in the Earth system | Kleidon (2009), DOI-10.1007/s00114-009-0509-x. A review of MEP in the Earth system. MEP is the proposed principle that a system with enough degrees of freedom adopts the steady state of maximum entropy production. It selects among steady states, where Prigogine's principle only describes relaxation toward one. Box models show the flux–force trade-off that gives an MEP state. The review estimates the Earth's entropy budget, which is dominated by absorption of sunlight. It surveys MEP fits for atmosphere, ocean, mantle, hydrology and biota, and proposes that life drives the planet toward MEP, a thermodynamic reading of Gaia. The author grants that MEP is not established. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-423](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-423.md)); worth reading as the clearest statement of the maximum-entropy-production (MEP) programme in Earth-system science by its main advocate: what MEP claims, how it differs from Prigogine's minimum principle (minimum entropy production describes relaxation toward a steady state; MEP selects among possible steady states), an order-of-magnitude entropy budget of the Earth, a survey of climate, ocean, mantle and biotic MEP applications, and the extension to life and Gaia. Read it as advocacy that is candid about its footing: the author calls MEP "proposed" and says "no one would argue that MEP is well established". Chosen over the Kleidon–Lorenz 2005 book, which has no lawful open text. |
| [LIT-520](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-520.md) | Maximum entropy production principle in physics, chemistry and biology | Martyushev & Seleznev (2006), DOI-10.1016/j.physrep.2005.12.001. A 45-page Physics Reports review of the maximum entropy production principle (MEPP) across physics, chemistry and biology. Kleidon (2009) cites it as the review of MEP's physical foundation. Semantic Scholar's machine-generated summary says it analyses the principle's thermodynamic and statistical basis, including its relation to the second law and to Prigogine's principle. Unread: no text or abstract reached. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from Crossref metadata and citing works, not read: no lawful full text or publisher abstract could be reached (Physics Reports, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy, and the abstract is elided by the publisher). Filed because it is the main survey of the maximum-entropy-production principle and of its relation to Prigogine's minimum principle; it stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-521.md) | Information theory explanation of the fluctuation theorem, maximum entropy production and self-organized criticality in non-equilibrium stationary states | Dewar (2003), DOI-10.1088/0305-4470/36/3/303. It applies Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference to the microscopic paths of an open system in a stationary state. Under fixed initial densities and boundary fluxes plus local conservation, the path distribution is p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ), with A_Γ carrying τσ_Γ/2k_B (Eq. 14). A fluctuation theorem and ⟨σ⟩ ≥ 0 follow (Eqs. 18–21). Then, in a mean-field approximation and assuming the number of paths increases with irreversible action, maximizing path entropy over the remaining multipliers is maximizing mean entropy production (MaxEP, Eq. 24). A Landau–Ginzburg argument claims self-organized criticality as slow driving goes to zero. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-426](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-426.md)); worth reading as the founding attempt to derive the maximum-entropy-production principle (MaxEP) from Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference over microscopic paths, and as the source most later MEP work, Kleidon's included, cites for MEP's theoretical foundation. Read it as a programme, not a proof. The path distribution p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ) and its fluctuation theorem follow from the stated constraints. The MaxEP step needs a mean-field approximation and an assumption that the number of paths grows with their irreversible action, which is stated, not argued. The self-organized-criticality corollary is a mean-field artefact by Grinstein and Linsker's analysis ([LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md)), which this reading confirms. |
| [LIT-524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-524.md) | Self-Organization in Nonequilibrium Systems: From Dissipative Structures to Order through Fluctuations | Nicolis & Prigogine (1977), Wiley-Interscience. The Brussels school's monograph on self-organization far from equilibrium, from the thermodynamics and bifurcation theory of dissipative structures to their stochastic theory ("order through fluctuations"). The Nobel lecture cites its ch. VII for the Brusselator and the book for its catalogue of chemical and biological examples. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the Brussels school's book-length treatment of dissipative structures and "order through fluctuations", and the source the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)) gives for the Brusselator; what it contains beyond that is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md) | Comments on a derivation and application of the ‘maximum entropy production’ principle | Grinstein & Linsker (2007), DOI-10.1088/1751-8113/40/31/N01. A Comment with two points. (1) Dewar's 2005 derivation of MaxEP needs a quadratic approximation to p(f) near f = F to hold for all f. With the fluctuation theorem, that forces A(F) to be constant, i.e. linear constitutive relations. So the "orthogonality condition" behind both maximum and minimum entropy production fails far from equilibrium, as an exact spin-chain model shows. (2) Dewar's 2003 SOC result is an artefact. Keeping the quartic term gives a finite flux variance at F_ext = 0. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-422](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-422.md)); worth reading as the short, exact critique of Dewar's information-theoretic derivation of maximum entropy production. It shows that the 2005 derivation's key step holds only where the constitutive relations are linear, so MaxEP far from equilibrium is not established by it, and that the 2003 claim that MaxEP yields self-organized criticality is an artefact of a mean-field expansion. Read from the authors' submitted manuscript (Zenodo); the version of record was not seen. Its first point is checked here only on its own worked example, since Dewar 2005 itself could not be read. |
| [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |
| [LIT-527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-527.md) | Pattern formation outside of equilibrium | Cross & Hohenberg (1993), DOI-10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851. A 262-page review classifying non-equilibrium patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state: type I_s (finite wave-number, stationary: convection rolls, Turing patterns), III_o (uniform oscillation: the stirred BZ reaction) and I_o (travelling waves). Near threshold, universal amplitude equations describe them, and phase equations describe them further above it. It finds no general variational principle for non-equilibrium steady states, only perturbative ones near threshold. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-418](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-418.md)), about 30 of 262 pages read closely; worth reading as the physicists' standard account of pattern formation away from equilibrium, and as the sober counterweight to the dissipative-structure programme. It treats Rayleigh–Bénard convection, Turing patterns and the BZ reaction in one framework, classifying patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state and describing them near onset by universal amplitude equations. Its conclusion finds "no evidence for the existence of any global minimization principles controlling the structure, except as a perturbative statement near threshold", and quotes Glansdorff and Prigogine conceding as much. |
| [LIT-528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-528.md) | Energy flow and the organization of life | Morowitz & Smith (2006 working paper; Complexity 2007). Life may be forced into existence by abiotic free-energy sources, as lightning and hurricanes are channels that relieve electric and thermal potentials. Core anabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle and the cascade built on it, is read as a relaxation channel for geochemical redox and phosphate energy. Jaynes-style entropy maximization with current-dependent entropies (not entropy-production principles) is offered as the framework, and the emergence of life as a "collapse", a phase transition of a metastable abiotic earth. Selection on metabolism comes before replication. No quantitative model is given; the authors say the claim is undemonstrated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-425](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-425.md)), from the Santa Fe Institute working paper (2006-08-029, dated 7 August 2006), not the Complexity version of record. Filed in place of Morowitz's 1968 book Energy Flow in Biology, which could not be read: every Internet Archive scan of it is lending-only. Worth reading as a short statement of the "life was inevitable" view by Morowitz and Smith: core metabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle, is a channel geochemistry was forced to open to relieve free-energy stresses, as lightning relieves a charge separation. It is an essay. It says itself that the claim "has not been quantitatively demonstrated", and its evidence is the structure of core metabolism read in that light. It puts life on a continuum with lightning and hurricanes and draws no principled line. |
| [LIT-529](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-529.md) | Incomplete Nature: How Mind Emerged from Matter | Deacon (2011), W. W. Norton. An account of how life, mind and purpose ("ententional" phenomena) emerged from physics, built on constraint and absence rather than on added stuff. Its contents run from absence, homunculi and teleonomy through emergence and constraint to a hierarchy of dynamics (homeodynamics, morphodynamics, teleodynamics), a minimal self-producing system (autogenesis), and then work, information, significance, evolution, self, sentience and consciousness. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the contents; the text was not reached. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan of the Norton printing is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found. The companion chapter the record already cites, Deacon & Cashman (2013), "Teleology versus mechanism in biology: beyond self-organization", is identified below but was not reachable either and is not filed. |
| [LIT-530](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-530.md) | What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell | Schrödinger (1944), Cambridge University Press. Lectures given at Trinity College Dublin in February 1943, published as a short book for the lay reader. It asks how events inside a living organism can be accounted for by physics and chemistry. It treats the gene as an "aperiodic crystal" carrying a code-script, defended through the Delbrück model, and in chapter 6 says an organism keeps its order by drawing "order from order" and by feeding on negative entropy from its surroundings. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and contents; the text itself was not reached. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Cambridge Core contents and chapter excerpts, and library catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The book is in copyright with Cambridge University Press. Every Internet Archive scan of a Cambridge or Macmillan printing is lending-only, and the freely downloadable PDFs that turn up (course sites, personal uploads, Internet Archive "opensource" uploads) are unauthorized copies of the Canto edition, so I did not open them. Chapter 6, the negative-entropy chapter, is unread beyond the publisher's one-paragraph excerpt. |
| [LIT-531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-531.md) | Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction | Zhabotinsky (2007), Scholarpedia 2(9):1435. BZ reactions are metal-ion-catalysed oxidations of organic reductants by bromate in acid. The core loop is autocatalytic oxidation of the catalyst via HBrO₂, switched off by bromide, which the oxidized catalyst regenerates from bromomalonic acid. Closed, stirred, it can run "up to several thousand" cycles; only in a continuous-flow reactor do oscillations continue indefinitely, and there bursting and chaos appear. Unstirred thin layers support target and spiral waves (Zaikin & Zhabotinsky 1970). The Oregonator is qualitatively right and quantitatively not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-414](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-414.md)); worth reading as the short, authoritative account of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction by the chemist who named half of it: discovery, the core mechanism (autocatalytic HBrO₂ inhibited by Br⁻), the Oregonator and its known defects, closed versus open-reactor dynamics, and target and spiral waves. Chosen over Zaikin & Zhabotinsky (1970) because it is openly readable and covers the 1970 waves paper; it is a short encyclopedia review with no new results. |
| [LIT-532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-532.md) | Inadequacy of entropy and entropy derivatives in characterizing the steady state | Landauer (1975), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevA.12.636. Per its abstract: in a bistable system the kinetics of transitions between the two locally stable states can be changed without changing the behaviour near either state, so no quantity that characterises only the vicinity of the states can determine which is more probable. Separately, even a monostable linear circuit's steady state need not be one of minimum entropy production. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from its abstract and Crossref metadata, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Physical Review A, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy). Filed because it is the classic objection to entropy-based characterisations of nonequilibrium steady states, Prigogine's minimum principle among them; it stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-533.md) | Life as a manifestation of the second law of thermodynamics | Schneider & Kay (1994), Math. Comput. Modelling 19(6–8):25–48. A "restated second law": systems moved from equilibrium "utilize all avenues available to counter the applied gradients". Bénard convection and a vortex draining a bottle are read as structures that destroy gradients faster. Life is "another means of dissipating the solar induced gradient" (living systems as "sophisticated mini-tornados, with a memory"), and ecosystems develop to degrade more incoming exergy. A stressed marsh shows smaller flows and fewer cycles; airborne thermal scans show mature forests cooler (degrading 90% of net solar radiation against a quarry's 62%). The second law is "necessary but not sufficient" for life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-415](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-415.md)), from the authors' own formatted text (copyright line "James J. Kay and Eric Schneider, 1992"), not the journal's typeset version. Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |
| [LIT-534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-534.md) | Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature | Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Bantam; based on their La nouvelle alliance. A book for general readers that sets the science of complexity and irreversibility against classical dynamics. By its contents: the rise and limits of Newtonian science and its philosophical reception (Diderot, Kant, Hegel, Bergson, Whitehead); thermodynamics from Carnot to Boltzmann's order principle; linear and far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics, bifurcations and order through fluctuations; and the rediscovery of time in physics. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and a partial contents note; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the Bantam and Flamingo printings are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the popular and philosophical statement of the programme whose technical core is the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)); what it argues, beyond its contents, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-535.md) | The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis | Turing (1952), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1952.0012. Chemicals ("morphogens") that react and diffuse through tissue can turn a stable homogeneous state unstable, with random disturbances setting which pattern grows. On a ring of cells the linearized onset takes six forms. The most important is stationary waves of finite "chemical wave-length", which (9.4a, b) allow for two morphogens only if they diffuse at different rates. A 20-cell example computed on the Manchester computer gives a three-lobed pattern. Hydra tentacles, whorled leaves, dappling and gastrulation are suggested applications, not tested ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-427](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-427.md)); worth reading as the founding paper of reaction–diffusion pattern formation and the origin of what the Brussels school later called the "Turing bifurcation". A homogeneous, stable steady state of reacting and diffusing chemicals can be destabilized by diffusion itself and settle into a stationary pattern with an intrinsic "chemical wave-length". The analysis is linear and near onset by design, every biological application is offered as suggestion, and the paper says outright that its patterns are "dynamic equilibria" fed by "a continual supply of free energy", which places them among dissipative structures before the term existed. |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the chapter list. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read. The book is not open access at Springer, but the authors deposited a copy of it in HAL (hal-01151449, "Book_Autonomy_web.pdf", CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015). HAL now serves files behind an anti-bot challenge that requires a browser running JavaScript, and it states that the challenge is there against automated scrapers, so I did not try to get past it. A human reader can open the copy lawfully, and a reading from it would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-537](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-537.md) | Thermodynamic Theory of Structure, Stability and Fluctuations | Glansdorff & Prigogine (1971), Wiley-Interscience. The monograph of the Brussels thermodynamic stability theory. By the Nobel lecture's citations, it treats local equilibrium (ch. II), the second-order excess entropy δ²S as a Lyapounov function near equilibrium (ch. V), and the excess-entropy-production criterion far from equilibrium, including convection (ch. VII). Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the monograph in which Glansdorff and Prigogine set out the thermodynamic stability theory that the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)) summarizes; what it contains beyond what the lecture and Cross & Hohenberg cite from it is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md) | Explanatory Models for Psychiatric Illness | Kendler (2008), American Journal of Psychiatry 165(6):695–702. Psychiatry should explain by mechanisms, not laws. Psychiatric causes act at many levels, within and outside the person, and are non-aggregative and loop-ridden, as an alcohol-dependence sketch shows (gene–environment interaction, tolerance feedback, niche selection, aversive cultural transmission). So "hard reductionism" and "hard emergentism" both fail, but locally decomposable subsystems can still be studied and then reassembled. After Marr, biology will implement psychological functions, not replace them. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-432.md)), from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central; filed as the readable substitute for Kendler's 2005 "Toward a Philosophical Structure for Psychiatry" ([LIT-552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-552.md)), which has no lawful open copy. It opens by citing the 2005 paper for its premise that etiological models must be pluralistic, and develops two of the 2005 abstract's propositions at length: piecemeal integration becomes "decomposition and reassembly" of multilevel mechanisms, and the mind–brain question becomes Marr-style implementation, in which "biology will implement but not replace psychology". It does not restate the 2005 paper's arguments against dualism and epiphenomenalism, so it stands in for the pluralism, not for the whole of the earlier paper. |
| [LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md) | A Network Theory of Mental Disorders | Borsboom (2017), World Psychiatry 16(1):5–13. Mental disorders are not common causes of their symptoms but states of networks of symptoms that cause one another, through "myriads of biological, psychological and societal mechanisms". Five principles; the dynamic one is hysteresis: a strongly connected network, once activated by an external trigger, can sustain itself after the trigger is gone. Disorder is an alternative stable state of a strongly connected network, mental health the stable state of a weakly connected one. Comorbidity follows from bridge symptoms. Treatments are symptom, external-field or network interventions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-435](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-435.md)); worth reading as the short, citable statement of the network theory of mental disorders by its main author. Five principles: disorders are complex systems of interacting components, the components are the symptoms of the diagnostic manuals, the network comes from direct causal connections between symptoms, disorders are the tightly connected clusters, and disorders arise through hysteresis, so a strongly connected network can stay "stuck" after its trigger is gone. Mental health, disorder, resilience and vulnerability are redefined as stable states and dispositions of weakly or strongly connected networks. Its evidence is indirect and it says so: the theory is offered as an "organizing framework" and a deliberate simplification, and the strict symptom-component correspondence of principle 2 is its own flagged weak point. |
| [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Closure grounds teleology and normativity in the current system, unifying etiological and dispositional accounts. Flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes have closure but no functions, because each makes a single undifferentiated contribution to its own maintenance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-444.md)), from the HAL deposit of the submitted version. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | De Jaegher & Di Paolo (2007), Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 6(4):485–507. Coordination between coupled systems is cheap and common. When patterns of coordination and the course of an encounter shape each other, the interaction acquires its own operationally closed, precarious organization. Social interaction is then regulated coupling between autonomous agents that constitutes an autonomous relational organization without destroying the agents' autonomy. Because sense-making is embodied in movement, interactors can coordinate their sense-making, along a spectrum from modulated individual sense-making to jointly created meaning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md)), from the published version posted on De Jaegher's own site. Worth reading as the founding statement of participatory sense-making. A social interaction is defined as regulated coupling between autonomous agents that itself becomes an autonomous organization in the relational domain, without destroying the agents' autonomy; coordinating sense-making in interaction can generate meanings neither individual had. The argument is conceptual, illustrated by everyday cases and by the perceptual-crossing experiments; nothing is measured in the paper. |
| [LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md) | Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior | Kelso (1995), Dynamic Patterns: The Self-Organization of Brain and Behavior, MIT Press, xvii + 334 pp. The book-length statement of coordination dynamics. Unread: registered from catalogue records. What the record knows of its content comes from the works that cite it: the coordination potential of the HKB model (reproduced in Kelso 2021, Box 1), absolute versus relative coordination (De Jaegher & Di Paolo 2007, citing p. 98), a chapter on how HKB arose (ch. 3) and one on brain rhythms (ch. 8), per Kelso 2021. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book has no DOI, is not listed as open access, and MIT Press's page refused an automated request. Under the owner's rule for books it is supplanted by a shorter work by the same author, Kelso's 2021 retrospective on the HKB model ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)), which was read. It is filed because it is the citation others reach for when they mean coordination dynamics, relative coordination or metastability; De Jaegher & Di Paolo ([LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md)) and Raja et al. ([LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md)) both cite it. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md) | A theoretical model of phase transitions in human hand movements | Haken, Kelso & Bunz (1985), Biological Cybernetics 51(5):347–356. The HKB model, as described by Kelso 2021 ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)): relative phase φ between two rhythmically moving fingers is the order parameter, with potential V(φ) = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ; anti-phase coordination loses stability as movement frequency rises and the hands switch to in-phase, and the φ dynamics is derived from two nonlinearly coupled oscillators. Unread: registered from metadata and a secondary account. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03, not read. No lawful full text was found. Unpaywall lists the article as closed; Springer's page offers it only by subscription or purchase; Europe PMC has the record (PMID 3978150) without full text; no author or repository deposit turned up in a web search. The read substitute is Kelso's 2021 retrospective on the model ([LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md)), which gives the model's equations and regimes. A reader with Springer access could read the ten pages and promote this. |
| [LIT-598](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-598.md) | The Markov blanket trick: On the scope of the free energy principle and active inference | Raja, Valluri, Baggs, Chemero & Anderson (2021), Physics of Life Reviews 39:49–72. Restating the FEP's derivation (Langevin dynamics, NESS, Helmholtz decomposition, Markov blanket, variational bound), the authors grant that it is true of things so defined. But blankets apply to every "thing", not everything (the candle flame is excluded); the partition is placed by modelling convenience; relational properties (heading, affordances) and constitutive self-organization (a membrane the cell makes) fall outside it. The blanket's real role is to supply the partition variational Bayes needs. Active inference presupposes perception and action in its generative models. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-450](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-450.md)), from the authors' PhilSci-Archive preprint (March 2021); the Physics of Life Reviews version was not seen. Worth reading as the scope critique of the free energy principle: granted its premises the principle is true, but it applies only to "things" already given a Markov-blanket partition, the partition is placed where the model needs it, and relational properties and constitutive self-organization fall outside it. The blanket is a "trick" that lets any thing be modelled as a variational autoencoder. Active inference, as a process theory, presupposes perception and action in the generative model it is handed. |
| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. Noise, symmetry breaking (Δω) and metastability extend it; with Kuramoto's model it becomes a generalized HKB for many agents. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |
| [LIT-638](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-638.md) | Interacting spiral wave patterns underlie complex brain dynamics and are related to cognitive processing | Xu, Long, Feng & Gong (2023), Nature Human Behaviour 7:1196–1215. In Human Connectome Project fMRI (100 subjects per cohort), the phase field of slow cortical fluctuations holds about 16–19 rotating spirals at a time, centred on phase singularities that drift superdiffusively and sit on boundaries between functional regions. Opposite spirals annihilate, like ones repel. Spiral locations and rotation directions decode four language-task conditions at about 48% (chance 25%, matched raw-signal decoder 30%), and spiral arrays route task activity flow bottom-up while listening and top-down while answering. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-502](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-502.md)); worth reading as the claim that slow (0.01–0.1 Hz) human cortical fMRI fluctuations self-organise into many mobile, interacting spiral waves around phase singularities, as in excitable media and turbulence, and that their locations and rotation directions are task-specific and steer large-scale activity flow. The detection is careful about filtering artefacts (phase-randomised null, filtered–unfiltered similarity); the functional claims are correlational, the spatial scale was chosen to maximise task decoding, and the "gate" and "wall" rules are read off streamlines and a phase-oscillator lattice, not tested by perturbation. |
| [LIT-645](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-645.md) | Ultraviolet Superradiance from Mega-Networks of Tryptophan in Biological Architectures | Babcock et al. (2024), J. Phys. Chem. B 128(17):4035–4046, [ARXIV-2302.01469](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01469). Modelling tryptophan 1La transition dipoles in tubulin architectures with a radiative non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in the single-excitation limit, the authors predict strongly superradiant states (up to about 4000 times the single-tryptophan rate in a centriole, about 7000 extrapolated for large axon-like bundles) and a thermal quantum yield that rises with network size and survives static disorder of room-temperature size. Lifetimes, and so radiative rates, were not measured. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-509](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-509.md)); worth reading as the measured, room-temperature part of the case for collective quantum optical states in microtubules: a radiative-Hamiltonian model of up to more than 10⁵ tryptophan transition dipoles in microtubules, centrioles and axon-like bundles predicts superradiant states and a quantum yield that grows with network size, and steady-state spectroscopy finds the tryptophan quantum yield of microtubules (17.6 ± 2.1%) above that of free tubulin dimers (10.6 ± 0.6%). A review of neural traveling waves within single cortical areas, chiefly visual cortex: how circuits generate them, and how, by embedding sensory history in the evolving activity across a sensory map, they may implement spatiotemporal computations such as predicting upcoming input. It ends with a framework for generative processing by waves over sensory maps. Unread: registered from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the PubMed abstract, keywords and the Crossref record, not read. No lawful full text could be found: the article is not open access at Cell Press (Crossref gives the accepted manuscript an Elsevier open-access licence only from 2 September 2027), it is not in PubMed Central, Europe PMC lists no preprint, arXiv has none under Muller with this title, Unpaywall and OpenAlex list no repository copy, and Semantic Scholar marks it closed. | [LIT-707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-707.md) | Aggregativity: Reductive Heuristics for Finding Emergence | Wimsatt (1997), Philosophy of Science 64(S4):S372–S384. Unread. Per its abstract: most scientists call a system property emergent if it depends on the parts' mode of organisation, a view consistent with reduction. Emergence is the failure of aggregativity, the state in which "the whole is nothing more than the sum of its parts". Aggregativity needs four conditions; met differently for different decompositions and in degrees, they give criteria for choosing decompositions and heuristics for detecting the biases of "vulgar reductionisms". | Deferred — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Philosophy of Science's PSA supplement is paywalled at Cambridge Core and JSTOR, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and neither the 1997 paper nor its 2000 expansion is posted on Wimsatt's department pages. Content here is the publisher's abstract and Wimsatt's own summary in "Reductionism and its heuristics" (Synthese 2006), which his department posts and which was read in part. A person with library access could supply it; a reading would move this to Active and should state the four conditions exactly. |
| [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | Goulet, Erill, Ascunce, Finley & Javan (2020), Frontiers in Physiology 11:566968, a review. A coral is a consortium: the animal plus the Symbiodiniaceae, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses in its body, mucus and skeleton, and neighbours are excluded by definition. Membership can change, so one colony may be a different holobiont at different times. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. Whether the holobiont is the unit of selection is asked, not answered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md)); worth reading as a short, explicit statement of why a coral should be studied as a composite of host and microbes rather than as an animal with passengers. It is a mini-review with no data of its own (about 3,700 words), and its strongest point is conceptual: traits such as thermal tolerance belong to host–symbiont combinations, not to either partner. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. It poses, and does not answer, whether the coral holobiont is a unit of selection. |
| [LIT-710](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-710.md) | Signaling cascades and the importance of moonlight in coral broadcast mass spawning | Kaniewska, Alon, Karako-Lampert, Hoegh-Guldberg & Levy (2015), eLife 4:e09991. Acropora millepora colonies from Heron Island, held in outdoor tanks for the eight days before the 2011 spawning night, spawned with the reef under ambient night light (21:30–22:30). They did not spawn that night under added light after sunset (N = 5) or under darkness (N = 5). 184 transcripts varied only on the spawning day, rose around gamete release in ambient colonies, did not change in dark ones and changed early in lit ones. Spawning-night genes were enriched for G-protein-coupled signalling; the proposed melanopsin and neuropeptide cascade is untested. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-557](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-557.md)); worth reading as the record's one experiment in which an environmental cue is manipulated and a collective biological timing event fails. Colonies of Acropora millepora held in outdoor tanks spawned with the reef only under natural night light. Colonies given artificial light after sunset, and colonies kept dark, did not spawn that night (N = 6, 5, 5). A second experiment found that blue, green and white nocturnal light delayed spawning by 6–8 h or 2 nights and red light did not. The signalling cascade (melanopsin-like opsins, neuropeptide G-protein-coupled receptors) is a model proposed from transcript changes and is not tested. The study shows each colony tracking a shared cue; it does not test coordination between colonies. |
| [LIT-711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-711.md) | Phase Shifts, Herbivory, and the Resilience of Coral Reefs to Climate Change | Hughes et al. (2007), Current Biology 17(4):360–365. A replicated fish-exclusion experiment at Orpheus Island, Great Barrier Reef, begun in 2000 after the 1998 mass bleaching: four roofless 5 × 5 m cages, four partial cages and four open plots, over 30 months. Excluding large and medium fishes produced a phase shift to Sargassum-dominated macroalgae. Coral recovery was suppressed, through about two-thirds lower recruitment and more than double the mortality of surviving colonies. In the controls, coral cover nearly doubled to 20%, mainly by recruitment of taxa that bleaching had removed locally. Reopened cages lost their macroalgae within 30 days. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-558.md)), main text and methods; the supplement was out of reach. Worth reading as the controlled experiment behind the claim that reef recovery after bleaching depends on an ecological interaction, not only on surviving corals. On an inshore Great Barrier Reef crest after the 1998 bleaching, roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of four 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae rose to a mean of 56% cover in the cages against 4.1% and 1.7% in partial cages and open plots. Coral cover in the cages rose only from 6.0% to 7.7%, against 19.2% and 20.2%, because recruitment was about two-thirds lower and mortality of established colonies more than double. It is one site with four replicates per treatment. The cages excluded all large and medium fishes, not herbivores alone, and the macroalgal state vanished within 30 days of reopening them. |
| [LIT-712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-712.md) | Defining Coral Bleaching as a Microbial Dysbiosis within the Coral Holobiont | Boilard, Dubé, Gruet, Mercière, Hernandez-Agreda & Derome (2020), Microorganisms 8(11):1682, a review. Bleaching, the breakdown of the coral–dinoflagellate symbiosis, is redefined as a succession of three holobiont dysbiosis stages: (i) the microbiota buffers the stress and keeps essential functions; (ii) the algal partners are reorganised by shuffling or switching, with or without transient bleaching; (iii) the stress exceeds both buffers, symbionts are lost for good, opportunists invade and the coral dies, and at reef scale algae take over. The stages are a proposal, with no criteria to tell them apart, and the authors concede that microbial shifts are not shown to cause bleaching. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-556](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-556.md)); worth reading as the statement of the "adaptive dysbiosis" account of coral bleaching, which treats bleaching as three successive holobiont states: microbial buffering, reorganisation of the algal partners by shuffling or switching, and an irreversible breakdown ending in death. It is a review with no data of its own, and the account is a proposal. Its own text says that bacterial shifts during bleaching cannot yet be read as cause or consequence, so the title's "microbial dysbiosis" claims more than the body supports. |
| [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md) | The Method of Characteristics Revisited: A Viability Approach | Aubin (1999), lecture notes on arXiv. A set K is viable under a system if from each state in K at least one evolution stays in K, and invariant if every evolution does. By Nagumo's theorem K is viable exactly when the dynamics point into K's contingent cone at each state. The viability kernel of K is the largest viable subset of K; its complement in K is a repeller. The capture basin of a target is the set of states from which it can be reached in finite time. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-576](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-576.md)): the introduction and chapters 1–2 of the author's arXiv lecture notes, the parts that define viability. Worth reading as the shortest first-hand statement the record holds of Aubin's viability concepts: a set is viable if from every state at least one evolution stays in it, invariant if all do, and the viability kernel is the largest viable subset of a constraint set. Chapters 3 onward apply these to Hamilton–Jacobi equations and were not read. Stands in for the unread monograph [LIT-738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-738.md). |
| [LIT-720](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-720.md) | Catastrophic shifts in ecosystems | Scheffer, Carpenter, Foley, Folke & Walker (2001), Nature 413:591–596. Lakes, coral reefs, oceans, forests and arid lands can switch abruptly to a contrasting state, and loss of resilience usually paves the way. Unread: the theory and the criteria for demonstrating alternative states are read in the authors' 2003 review [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text was found (Nature is closed; no repository or course copy was located). The authors' 2003 review ([LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md)), read in full, restates its theory of alternative stable states and gives the criteria for showing one exists. Filed because it is the paper usually cited for catastrophic regime shifts. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md) | Catastrophic regime shifts in ecosystems: linking theory to observation | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), Trends in Ecology & Evolution 18:648–656. A regime shift can come from a bifurcation, not only a large shock. Field data give hints that are never conclusive. Experiments can demonstrate alternative attractors: initial states fixing end states, a temporary disturbance causing a lasting shift, or hysteresis. Positive feedbacks must be strong enough. Slow return can mimic a new state, as when a biomanipulated lake stayed clear for six years and then slipped back. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-571.md)): in full, from a UC Berkeley course page. Worth reading for its standard of evidence for alternative stable states. Field patterns (jumps in time series, multimodal distributions, dual relationships to a driver) are only hints. Experiments are what demonstrate: different initial states lead to different end states, a temporary disturbance causes a lasting shift, or the response to forward and backward change shows hysteresis. Positive feedback is not enough unless strong. Long return times can mimic an alternative state. |
| [LIT-738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-738.md) | Viability Theory | Aubin (1991; reprinted 2009), Birkhäuser: the monograph that founds viability theory, the study of which evolutions of a dynamical or controlled system can remain in a given constraint set, and of the set of initial states from which one can. Unread: registered from metadata; the definitions are read in Aubin's 1999 mini-course notes [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref and the author's own list of his books, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Springer serves the 2009 reprint behind a bot challenge, which was not passed. Aubin's 1999 mini-course notes ([LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md), read) state the definitions this book is cited for: a viable evolution, viability and invariance, the viability kernel and the capture basin. Filed because an essay the owner is writing cites "Aubin's mathematical theory of viability" for the difference between stability and viability. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md) | Resilience and Stability of Ecological Systems | Holling (1973), Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 4:1–23. Stability is how quickly and smoothly a system returns to equilibrium after a disturbance. Resilience is its ability to absorb change in state variables, drivers and parameters and still persist, a matter of the size of its domain of attraction. A system can be highly resilient and unstable, as the spruce budworm forest is. Managing for a stable maximum yield can shrink resilience until a rare event flips the system. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-572](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-572.md)): in full, from IIASA's authorised reprint. Worth reading as the origin of the distinction between stability and resilience. Stability is the speed and smoothness of return to an equilibrium after a disturbance. Resilience is the capacity to absorb change and still persist, measured by the size of the domain of attraction and how near its boundary the system sits. The two can trade off: management for constancy can erode resilience. Evidence is a set of case histories (lakes, spruce budworm, salmon, fire), not tests. |
| [LIT-743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-743.md) | Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem | Rasmussen (1997), Safety Science 27:183–213. Risk management is a control problem spanning government, regulators, companies, management, staff and work. Behaviour within a work space moves under an effort gradient and a cost gradient toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems, defences degrade unobserved under cost pressure. Accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions. Improvement means making boundaries visible, not fighting errors. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md)): the argument in full, the review of research paradigms skimmed, from the author's manuscript in DTU's repository. Worth reading for the model of drift. Under a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from workers, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems one actor's breach of a defence has no visible effect, so defences erode unobserved. Major accidents come from the interaction of many decision makers adapting to local pressures, not from coincident errors. Built from accident analyses; not a quantitative model. |
| [LIT-746](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-746.md) | Brain of the Firm | Beer (1972), Brain of the Firm, Allen Lane; 2nd edn Wiley 1981. The streamlined statement of the Viable System Model in neurophysiological terms, the second edition adding the Chilean application of 1971–73. Unread: the model is read in Beer's 1984 retrospective [LIT-752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-752.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Open Library and Beer's own references, not read: no copy was sought, the book being in copyright and commercially published. Its model is read first-hand in Beer's article-length retrospective "The Viable System Model: Its Provenance, Development, Methodology and Pathology" ([LIT-752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-752.md)), which restates the five subsystems, the recursion theorem and the pathologies and refers to this book and The Heart of Enterprise for the detail. Filed because it is the book usually cited for the Viable System Model. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-752.md) | The Viable System Model: Its Provenance, Development, Methodology and Pathology | Beer (1984), Journal of the Operational Research Society 35:7–25. A retrospective on the Viable System Model. Any system able to keep its identity independently in a shared environment has five necessary and sufficient subsystems, and every viable system contains and is contained in one. The model is offered as a scientific model reached by homomorphic mapping, not an analogy. Breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem, as when Three and Five collapse without Four. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md)): in full except one page, from the 1989 book reprint posted by the Cwarel Isaf Institute, which Beer co-founded. Worth reading as Beer's own retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are claimed necessary and sufficient for any system to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs, since every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns are diagnosed as failures of a subsystem: without System Four, Systems Three and Five collapse into each other and the system can only react. Limits: the paper declines to expound or validate the model, the copy lacks the page with the synopsis of the subsystems and its figures, and the applications are recalled, not documented. |
